title: Arise, Awake: The Living Demonstration
reflection: Which of your own moods could you meet this week as weather, with yourself as the sky it passes through? What would change if you did?

questions.q: What is the point of the account of Manmatha Nath Ganguli, according to Conversation 5.8?
o: It shows that the framework describes something real that a person can actually pass through.
It proves that realisation can be forced by anyone who sits with a great teacher.
It shows that a person must first learn the whole framework before any recognition can come.
It shows that the experience is rare, and that the course is therefore only a story.
questions.e: Manmatha Nath knew none of the framework. He sat down to ask about māyā and lived, within minutes, the whole journey the course describes. The architecture describes something real that human beings actually traverse. This is the map made flesh.
questions.c: A real account shows that the framework describes a journey that is lived

questions.q: A reader notices that Manmatha Nath did nothing that afternoon except sit and listen, and asks how the recognition came. Which view fits Conversation 5.8?
o: He had practised for years in secret, and the afternoon was only the last step.
It was given: a presence resting at the source drew his mind into resonance with it.
He understood the argument so well that the understanding carried him to the end.
It was a trick of the mind, brought on by tiredness and by the teacher’s voice.
questions.e: In his own account the recognition came through the teacher’s grace. This is transmission, the strong form of what the company of the true does gently: a mind resting permanently at the source acts like a tuning fork and draws a nearby mind into resonance, far beyond what its own practice could reach that day.
questions.c: The recognition was given, like a tuning fork drawing a mind into step

questions.q: In Manmatha Nath’s account, what does the void he met stand for in the course’s picture?
o: An empty state in which nothing is left, and the person has gone out like a flame.
A deep sleep, from which the person wakes with nothing to say about it.
A pause in the senses only, which is of no further meaning for the person.
The screen with the film switched off: awareness, with nothing playing on it but itself.
questions.e: Swamiji says the void is not nothing. It is the screen with nothing playing on it but itself, the threshold. From there came the recognition of undivided consciousness, with himself and his teacher as two bubbles in one ocean. It was recognised, not produced.
questions.c: The void is the screen with the film switched off, not nothing

questions.q: From his height, Manmatha Nath says that all his teacher’s work, the schools and hospitals, is māyā, and asks why it is done. What is the heart of the reply in Conversation 5.8?
o: Yes, it is māyā, and he is playing with it: free within it, and not caught or fooled.
No, the work is quite real, and the student has not yet seen far enough.
The work is māyā, and so it should be given up in favour of withdrawal.
The question cannot be answered, and the student should wait until he understands.
questions.e: Swamiji gives a threefold reply: you have said aright; I am playing with māyā; and the cave remains a real alternative for those it suits. The work is poured out fully and held without grip. It is freedom in the world, not freedom from it.
questions.c: He affirms it is māyā and answers: I am playing with it, free within it

questions.q: “The recognition empties the work of meaning, so that a person who has seen it can no longer act with energy or care.”
questions.e: Kai’s question is answered the other way. The recognition does not empty the work of meaning; it empties it of grip, desperation and the fear that the outcome will make or break you. What is left is the freest and fullest kind of action there is: service offered as play.
questions.c: The recognition empties the work of grip, not of meaning

questions.q: A reader says the course itself must be false, since it too is within māyā. How does Conversation 5.8 reply?
o: The reader is right, so the course should be dropped for something that is not illusion.
The course is the truth itself, and so it is not a part of any illusion at all.
It is a pointing finger and not the moon, yet it is made of the same stuff as what it points to.
It is an illusion, and so it will serve only those who already believe it.
questions.e: The whole course is a pointing finger and not the moon. And the stairs are made of the very same material as the roof, so the framework is illusion and also a faithful expression of the real. Climbed with care, it raises you to where the truth can recognise itself.
questions.c: The course is a finger pointing, made of the same stuff as the moon

questions.q: A woman says, “I am an angry person,” and sees that she has taken a mood for who she is. Which step fits the call to awaken in Conversation 5.8?
o: Resolve to build a calmer self, bit by bit, until the angry one has been replaced.
See that she is the awareness the mood arises in, as the sky holds the storm.
Push the anger away at once, since it is the one thing that hides the Self.
Wait for a great experience that will show her what she really is, without effort.
questions.e: The sleep is one precise mistake: taking the passing contents of the mind, the thoughts, moods, body and little I, to be the whole of what you are. Awakening does not produce a new state; it recognises that the substrate was never the contents. You are not the waves.
questions.c: Awakening is seeing that she is the awareness the mood passes through

questions.q: “The practices manufacture the awakening, so that the Self is built up by breath, attention, action and knowledge working together.”
questions.e: None of the practices was manufacturing anything. They dissolve the obstructions: lowering the noise until what was always there can be heard, and lightening the filter until what was always shining can show through. The Self was never missing, and the practices are how the things hiding it quietly remove themselves.
questions.c: The practices clear what hides the Self; they do not build it

questions.q: A doctor asks what the whole course means for how she treats her patients. Which view fits Conversation 5.8?
o: Treat each patient as already whole beneath what hides it, and offer the stairs honestly.
Treat each patient as broken, and use the four doorways in turn until they are mended.
Treat the framework as the roof, and give it to each patient as the final answer.
Treat the patient’s belief as the key, and begin by asking what each of them believes.
questions.e: Dr Watson’s summary is the course in one sentence: we were never fixing what was broken, but clearing what hid what was never broken. Hold both lenses, measure what can be measured, and offer the stairs without pretending they are the roof.
questions.c: Patients are already whole beneath what hides it; offer the stairs honestly

questions.q: “The cave of withdrawal is a real and honourable path for those it suits, though it is not the only way, and it is not the one the course teaches.”
questions.e: Swami Vivekananda names the cave honestly as a genuine alternative, and does not argue against it. Himself, he chose freedom in the world: pouring himself fully into the work and holding it lightly. The path is real at every level at which it is walked.
questions.c: The cave is a real path for those it suits; this course walks another
